newsitem.title: USA: New tax law offers little for new business ventures.
newsitem.headline: New tax law offers little for new business ventures.

text.p: The new federal budget, despite its much-hyped tax cuts for investors and families, offers relatively little direct support for entrepreneurs launching new ventures, legal experts say.

While the capital gains tax reduction may induce some investors to take profits from successful investments and put the funds into new entrepreneurial ventures, other provisions of the law do little to encourage business formation.

"There's not a lot there for entrepreneurs," said David Lutgin, a family and business attorney with the McCarter & English law firm in Newark, N.J. "Something is better than nothing, but it's not as if this was a Christmas tree for entrepreneurs."

Legal experts say that except for the capital gains tax cuts, the primary entrepreneural issues addressed by the law are improved deductibility of health care expenses for the self-employed, and clearer rules on home-office deductibility.
"But the home office rules are still complicated, and all the rules regarding how you've got to prove that the home office is used for an office are still in place," said Lutgin.

Under the old regulations, if you spend a lot of time out of your home doing billing and administrative work, even if you have a fixed office in your home but still do a substantial amount of your business, say, from hotel rooms, you did not qualify for the home office exemption.

"The new bill clarifies that in determining whether your home office is your principle place of business, you don't take into account activities that are conducted outside of your home," said Rory Deutsch, a tax specialist with Roberts, Sheridan & Kotel, in New York.
"If you don't have a fixed office and your home is your fixed office, you will qualify for the home office deductions," he said.
Noting that the Internal Revenue Service has in the past viewed the home office deduction as a red flag, Deutsch said it's unclear whether the new law might reduce your susceptibility to an audit.

"If all your office mail comes to your home and it's clear you have no other office that you go to as a permanent place of business, my guess is that although the bill doesn't expressly address this, the IRS is likely to give this area less attention." he said.

While most small businesses are incorporated in one form or another, and thus could already deduct health care costs, the self-employed and those who run their businesses as sole proprietorships will benefit under the new law.

"They will be able to deduct an increasing percentage of their health insurance premiums, said Lutgin. But they'll have to be patient, as the improved provisions will only be phased in over several years.

One area that owners, managers and employees of new businesses should be cognizant of, particularly in ventures involving high-technology or bio-technology, Deutsch said, is the increased disparity between capital gains and ordinary income tax rates.

"Well-advised employees will want to minimize the ordinary income component of their pay package, which will be taxed at up to 40 percent, and maximize the capital gains component, which will be taxed at 20 percent if they hold shares for 18 months," he said.

Entrepreneurs who cash out of their businesses with large gains will benefit from the lower capital gains rate, as well as a provision in the law that allows for the rollover of gains from small business stock.
It could be that these features of the law will end up boosting new businesses.

"There are some tricky features to the rollover, in order to qualify for it," said Mike Guariglia, also of McCarter & English. "Some of the early commentary is suggesting that this will increase the availability of venture capital for new entrepreneurial ventures."
